en: Alooke’s son Kongurbay,
The fierce warrior rich in wisdom,
Stood apart from them.
Those eight mighty men standing there
Were seen by Sultan Manas Khan
From upon the rise.
“If you grant me those eight, one God,
Then load me upon a thoroughbred!
Let me have no cause for regret.
O one God, whom I adore,
Take back the life you entrusted me!
Do not make me a slayer of unbelievers;
Without letting me take blood from Beijing,
Do not lay me level with the black earth!
Beneath me, for me to mount and ride,
There is no swift horse like Akkula.
To stand and lend me help,
No brothers Almambet and Syrgak are here!”
Having spoken these words,
Your champion lord, the leopard,
Now took Akkelte in his hand.
At the eight champions before him
Your mighty warrior fixed his gaze.
As he leveled Akkelte,
As your Magnanimous One watched intently,
His two eyes seeming four,
Your warrior sultan burned with grief.
In the sight of Akkelte,
The precious heads of those eight
Hung like little buttons.
The longer he stared, the more they shimmered;
The eight drew near, a doorway’s height away.
When they came close without delay,
When your precious lord saw them,
Would he merely stand and stare?
Would God strike down the Blood-Shedder?
He struck the thunderous drum once—
Akkelte within his hand.
The precious lion, unmoving,
Fired Akkelte once.
Roaring, Kelte’s shot reached them;
Joykara and Kojojash,
With all eight sorcerers, were flung back.
From where it fired, Akkelte
Tore off their heads as it passed.
The mass of monks fled in panic
When they heard Akkelte’s voice,
When it felled their eight giants.
The Manchus fled in terror;
Chinese, Solon and Manchu
Scattered in separate bands.
Why would your noble one hold back?
Your lion Manas, that precious champion,
Stood trembling on the ridge,
Leaning upon Akkelte.
Then that beauty of dark complexion,
The radiant one among Muslims,
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykei,
Woke from her sleep in fright.
She turned onto her right side,
Dipped her hand into water,
And performed her ablution.
Your noble falcon rose at once,
Imploring her Bakai.
Her words to Allah were anguished pleas.
The torment of six months ahead—
Ready to tell it that very instant,
Beneath your sister-in-law’s arm
There dwelt a naked child.
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykei
Was a woman endowed with sacred power.
Unable even to sniff back her running nose,
Her ribs seeming to break apart,
Tears poured from her eyes.
Those dear quail-like eyes
Had seen an ominous dream;
Tears fell in separate streams.
“A blue bull with blunted horns
Bellows beneath the water.
My sultan Alma must have died!
The white falcon that drove off crows
Has been left without its wings.
Has Chubak, son of Khan Baltai,
Suffered some humiliation?
The tall plane tree
Has fallen toward the qibla.
Has my precious Syrgak died?
Over eighteen thousand worlds,
While he stood as khan,
The golden throne my sultan sat upon
Has had its legs shattered.
Has your gray-maned hero’s swift horse
Been struck down by a bullet?
Have the forty tribes of imperial China
Surrounded the Magnanimous One?
Has my king spoken his last wishes
And fallen into Chinese hands?
Your friend Manas, all alone—
Have the swarming Chinese reached him?
If this foreboding is true, your gray-maned friend Manas
Has been surrounded forty-two times by the Chinese!
If he lies unwatched in Beijing, he will die.
When will his hapless wife see her champion?
To Beijing, which even Chaliyar cannot reach,
The warrior’s strength is unequal: let him return!
To Beijing, where no prophet treads,
His standing does not suffice: let him return!
If my king will heed my words,
Let him set out this way in safety!
On the hills, the horses have piebald heads.
Let him not bring needless suffering:
My gray-maned hero’s young son is left behind.
Let him come safely home from Beijing!
His brothers, elder and younger, are all enemies.
The treachery of his kin shows in their eyes.
If they have the strength, the six scoundrels
Are bent on tripping you up.
Crookedness runs through their words;
Malice shows within their eyes.
Given the chance, the dog will cut you down;
Such are the deeds they plot against you.
Common iron cannot become fine steel;
Dogs raised elsewhere cannot become your people.”
Weeping and weeping, she wrote a letter:
“Let my champion lord return!
Let my warrior heed my words,
Let him yield to these troubled words!”
She gave six fleet horses,
With Arbuudan at their head,
And gave a letter the size of a palm.
Then the saintly warrior Bakai
Put on his blue lynx-fur cap,
His mottled blue shield swinging,
His head bathed in gold coins,
His feet supported by gleaming gold.
He who found a way in darkness,
Who found words when taken unawares,
Who never faltered amid turmoil,
In darkness, a corsac fox’s trail—
He would never lose it in pursuit.
Led Buurul beside him, plunging forward.
The horse was just reaching maturity;
That well-bred warhorse
Was fit to ride upon campaign.
Its short ribs stood out powerfully;
It had now come into its strength.
The renowned Arbuudan
Had now filled out completely.
The creature curved its neck like a stag;
When a ditch a bowshot wide appeared,
It raced across without delay.
Knowing it was a peerless steed,
Offering gold by the pood,
The khan of lower Bukhara had asked for it.
It was not given to the one who asked.
Far from giving Buurul away,
No one without ablution even rode it.
It curved its neck like a wild ram;
When a ditch a spear’s length wide appeared,
It raced across without hesitation.
Knowing its noble worth,
Khans from every quarter had asked for it.
Reared with care, it had become a horse;
Anyone who asked for it became a stranger to Manas.
Just as it reached maturity,
It was tied up again and kept close,
Entrusted to his only son Semetey.
Khan Bakai, with the blue winged steed,
Now plainly took it along beside him.
As they descended slopes,
Its forelegs struck out like a roe deer’s.
As they climbed uphill,
Its mane and tail spread wide.
Its hoof-soles clattered on the earth;
The bit of black steel
Clanged deep in the creature’s mouth.
Then Bakai the leopard,
With the two winged horses,
Raced against the flying birds.
The white reins, joined with rounded knots,
Stiffened in his hand beyond his power to pull.
With one of those peerless winged steeds
He wrestled for control of its mouth.
The ground it trod was shattered;
Stones as large as great cauldrons
Whistled overhead.
Its ravenous mouth gaped open;
White foam mixed with blood
Spattered across its breast.
They traveled day and night,
Covering great distances, sparing no horse,
Passing many stretches on the way.
Taking no sleep by day,
Taking no rest by night—
When the days were counted,
When the days were set down in writing,
They had traveled twelve days.
Lion Bakai grew eager;
At the ridge before him
He encountered a seething multitude.
In the haze where stars appeared,
What seemed stars proved to be fires.
The many dark shapes standing thickly—
What seemed a forest proved to be people.
The dark shapes swaying out there—
What seemed reeds proved to be a flood.
The dense blaze lost in haze—
What seemed tumbleweed proved to be people.
The countless Kalmyks, seething like worms,
Had surrounded the Muslims.
There lay a dark trench they had dug.
The shapes massed thickly before him—
What seemed a ridge proved to be people.
The many evil-hearted Chinese
Had brought your champion Manas
And the handful of the Islamic faith
Into desperate distress.
Then Prince Bakai’s
Thoughts were torn apart.
Those bitter tears mixed with blood—
“Where shall I find my khan?”—
Poured down past his collarbones.
His many worries overflowed his breast.
“Where shall I find the gray-maned one?”
His tears flowed every way.
“The youngest of the six lions—
The Chinese have shot and slaughtered him!
His bones lie unburied on the plain.
What has become of my Magnanimous One?
The support on which I girded my strength—
Have I been parted thus
From my lion, Magnanimous Manas?
What is seen today is gone tomorrow.
Was it you who kept deceiving us,
Damn your father’s grave, mischievous world!
My magnanimous lion favored by Khizr—
The Chinese must have bound him with shouts!
For the females in Beijing
They must have made my lord a breeding stallion!
I look, but he does not meet my eye;
I cannot tell which one he is.
The Chinese must have openly bound him
And before the imperial khan
Presented the leopard as a gift!”
Grieving Bakai wept bitterly,
Weeping, “My generous sultan!”
In the settlement of the tea-growing mountain,
Mighty Bakai kept stopping.
“Where is Manas, the other half of my soul?”
Warrior Bakai kept searching for him.
His friend Manas was not there;
Mighty Bakai kept searching for him.
Koktulpar, the horse beneath him,
Was whipped on by mighty Bakai.
Grieving for the leopard,
Among those fallen every which way,
